title: Periodic relationship
body: A periodic relationship exists between two aspects of a context if, as the input values increase, the output values show a repeating pattern over successive equal-length intervals.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 "output values demonstrate a repeating pattern over successive equal-length intervals"

title: Period of a periodic function
body: The period is the smallest positive value k such that f(x + k) = f(x) for all x in the domain, so any interval of width k completely determines the function's behavior.
caution: The period is the smallest such positive k, not just any k that repeats the pattern.
ced_evidence: 3.1.B.1 "smallest positive value k such that f(x+k)=f(x)"

title: Characteristics repeat in every period
body: All characteristics found in one period of a periodic function (intervals of increase and decrease, concavities, rates of change) appear in every period.
ced_evidence: 3.1.B.3 "all characteristics found in one period of the function will be in every period"

title: Angle in standard position and terminal ray
body: An angle is in standard position when its vertex is at the origin and one ray lies on the positive x-axis; the other ray is the terminal ray.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis"

title: Direction of angle rotation and coterminal angles
body: Positive angle measures rotate counterclockwise and negative measures rotate clockwise from the positive x-axis; angles in standard position with the same terminal ray differ by an integer number of revolutions.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "counterclockwise and clockwise direction, respectively"

title: Radian measure of an angle
body: \theta=\frac{s}{r}
caution: Here s is the arc length the angle subtends and r is the radius of the same circle. On a unit circle, one radian subtends an arc of length 1.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.2 "ratio of the length of the arc of the circle that the angle subtends to the radius"

title: Sine and cosine as ratios on a circle
body: \sin\theta=\frac{y}{r},\qquad \cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3 and 3.2.A.4 "for a unit circle, the sine of the angle is the y-coordinate of point P"; "the cosine of the angle is the x-coordinate"

title: Tangent as sine over cosine
body: \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},\quad \cos\theta\neq 0
caution: The tangent of an angle is also the slope of the terminal ray, if that slope exists.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.5 "the ratio of the angle's sine to its cosine"; 3.8.A.2

title: Coordinates of a point on a circle of radius r
body: P=(r\cos\theta,\; r\sin\theta)
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1 "The coordinates of point P are (r cos θ, r sin θ)"

hooks.hook_text: Cosine and sine go in alphabetical order, like x and y
hooks.when_to_use: When you need to remember which coordinate of the unit-circle point goes with cosine and which with sine.
hooks.caution: In your answer state that cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate of the point where the terminal ray meets the circle, and multiply by r when the radius is not 1.

title: Exact first-quadrant values of cosine and sine
body: Exact values come from isosceles right and equilateral triangles for multiples of pi/4 and pi/6; use the quadrant to set the sign.

items.label: \pi/6
items.meaning: \cos=\sqrt{3}/2,\ \sin=1/2

items.label: \pi/4
items.meaning: \cos=\sqrt{2}/2,\ \sin=\sqrt{2}/2

items.label: \pi/3
items.meaning: \cos=1/2,\ \sin=\sqrt{3}/2

caution: These are reference values for the first quadrant. For terminal rays in other quadrants, use the same magnitudes and attend to the signs.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.2 "exact values for the cosine and sine of angles that are multiples of π/4 and π/6"

title: Signs of cosine and sine by quadrant
body: The signs of cosine (x-coordinate) and sine (y-coordinate) are determined by the quadrant of the terminal ray.

items.label: Quadrant I
items.meaning: cos +, sin +

items.label: Quadrant II
items.meaning: cos -, sin +

items.label: Quadrant III
items.meaning: cos -, sin -

items.label: Quadrant IV
items.meaning: cos +, sin -

ced_evidence: 3.3.A.2 "attending to the signs of the values based on the quadrant of the angle"

hooks.when_to_use: When checking the sign of an exact value after finding its reference magnitude.
hooks.caution: In your answer, justify the sign using the x- and y-coordinates of the terminal-ray point in that quadrant, not the mnemonic.

title: Sine and cosine function domain and range
body: The sine and cosine functions have domain all real numbers, and their outputs oscillate between -1 and 1, taking every value in between, as they track the y- and x-coordinates of the point on the unit circle.
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.1-3.4.A.4 "oscillate between −1 and 1"; "The domain of the sine function is all real numbers"

title: Cosine as a phase shift of sine
body: \cos\theta=\sin\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.1 "cos θ = sin(θ + π/2)"

title: Period and frequency are reciprocals
body: \text{frequency}=\frac{1}{\text{period}};\quad \text{for }\sin\theta\text{ and }\cos\theta:\ \text{period}=2\pi,\ \text{frequency}=\frac{1}{2\pi}
caution: Do not use a frequency where a period is needed, or the reverse.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.2 "The period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals"

title: Amplitude of a sinusoidal function
body: \text{amplitude}=\frac{\text{maximum}-\text{minimum}}{2}
caution: The amplitude of sin and cos is 1.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3 "half the difference between its maximum and minimum values"

title: Midline of a sinusoidal function
body: y=\frac{\text{maximum}+\text{minimum}}{2}
caution: The midline of y = sin θ and y = cos θ is y = 0.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.4 "average, or arithmetic mean, of the maximum and minimum values"

title: Concavity of sinusoidal graphs
body: As the input increases, the graph of a sinusoidal function alternates between concave down and concave up.
caution: Describe concavity as concave up or concave down. Do not use rate-of-a-rate language such as "increasing at an increasing rate", which requires calculus.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.5 "oscillate between concave down and concave up"

title: Odd and even symmetry of sine and cosine
body: \sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\ \ (\text{odd, rotational symmetry about the origin}),\qquad \cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\ \ (\text{even, reflective symmetry over the }y\text{-axis})
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.6 "y = sin θ ... odd function ... y = cos θ ... even function"

title: General sinusoidal function form
body: f(\theta)=a\sin\bigl(b(\theta+c)\bigr)+d\quad\text{or}\quad g(\theta)=a\cos\bigl(b(\theta+c)\bigr)+d,\quad a\neq0,\ b\neq0

title: Reading a, b, c, d in a sinusoidal function
body: Characteristics of y = a sin(b(θ + c)) + d (same for cosine), with the transformation each parameter causes.

items.label: Amplitude
items.meaning: |a|; vertical dilation of the graph by a factor of |a|

items.label: Period
items.meaning: \frac{1}{|b|}\cdot 2\pi=\frac{2\pi}{|b|}; horizontal dilation by a factor of 1/|b|

items.label: Midline / vertical shift
items.meaning: d units from y = 0, so the midline is y = d

items.label: Phase shift
items.meaning: -c units (horizontal translation)

caution: The phase shift is -c, the opposite sign of c, and it applies only when the form is b(θ + c), with b factored out.
ced_evidence: 3.6.A.6 "amplitude of |a| units, a period of (1/|b|)2π units, a midline vertical shift of d units ... phase shift of −c units"

title: Converting frequency to the parameter b
body: b=2\pi f=\frac{2\pi}{\text{period}}
caution: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period. For example, 200 cycles per second gives b = 2π·200, not b = 200.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.2 "period and frequency ... are reciprocals"; 3.6.A.6 "a period of (1/|b|)2π"; 3.7.A.1

title: Building a sinusoidal model from data
body: Which data feature determines which parameter of a sinusoidal model.

items.label: Period and frequency
items.meaning: input-value interval between consecutive maxima or consecutive minima

items.label: Amplitude and vertical shift
items.meaning: from the maximum and minimum output values

items.label: Phase shift
items.meaning: compare an actual input-output pair with pairs the model produces

items.label: With technology
items.meaning: estimate key values or use a sinusoidal regression

title: Contextual domain for models and equations
body: A sinusoidal model is usually valid only over its contextual domain, and a domain implied by the context limits the number of solutions to equations and inequalities.
ced_evidence: 3.7.A.5 "frequently only useful over their contextual domain"; 3.10.A.3

title: Key characteristics of the tangent function
body: Characteristics of f(θ) = tan θ.

items.label: Meaning
items.meaning: slope of the terminal ray of the angle in standard position

items.label: Period
items.meaning: \pi (slope values repeat every half revolution)

items.label: Vertical asymptotes
items.meaning: \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi,\ k\text{ an integer}, where cos θ = 0

items.label: Behavior between consecutive asymptotes
items.meaning: increasing, changing from concave down to concave up

title: General tangent function form and period
body: f(\theta)=a\tan\bigl(b(\theta+c)\bigr)+d,\qquad \text{period}=\frac{1}{|b|}\pi=\frac{\pi}{|b|}
caution: The tangent's period is π/|b|, not 2π/|b|. Here d shifts the line through the points of inflection and the phase shift is −c.
ced_evidence: 3.8.C.5 "a period of (1/|b|)π units ... vertical shift of the line containing the points of inflection ... phase shift of −c"

title: Reflections in tangent transformations
body: For g(θ) = a tan θ, a < 0 reflects the graph over the x-axis; for g(θ) = tan(bθ), b < 0 reflects the graph over the y-axis.
ced_evidence: 3.8.C.3 "If a < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the x-axis"; 3.8.C.4

title: Restricted domains that define inverse trig functions
body: Domain restrictions that make sine, cosine, and tangent invertible.

items.label: Sine
items.meaning: \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]

items.label: Tangent
items.meaning: \left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)

ced_evidence: 3.9.A.3 "domain of the sine function is restricted to [−π/2, π/2], the cosine function to [0, π], and the tangent function to (−π/2, π/2)"

title: Inverse trigonometric functions (arcsine, arccosine, arctangent)
body: Inverse trigonometric functions, written arcsin x, arccos x, arctan x or sin⁻¹x, cos⁻¹x, tan⁻¹x, switch the inputs and outputs of the trig functions, so the input is a trig value and the output is often interpreted as an angle measure.
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1-3.9.A.2 "called arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent"

title: Solving trigonometric equations and inequalities
body: Inverse trig functions help solve trig equations and inequalities, but because trig functions are periodic there are often infinitely many solutions, and the inverse's output may need to be modified for the domain restriction.
caution: A single inverse-trig output is only one solution. Find the other solutions and check them against the stated or contextual domain.
ced_evidence: 3.10.A.1-3.10.A.2 "infinitely many solutions to trigonometric equations"

title: Secant, cosecant, and cotangent definitions
body:
\sec	heta= rac{1}{\cos	heta}\ (\cos	heta
eq0),\quad \csc	heta= rac{1}{\sin	heta}\ (\sin	heta
eq0),\quad \cot	heta= rac{1}{	an	heta}= rac{\cos	heta}{\sin	heta}\ (	an	heta
eq0,\ \sin	heta
eq0)

title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent
body: Key graph characteristics of the reciprocal trigonometric functions.

items.label: Secant
items.meaning: vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero; range (-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)

items.label: Cosecant
items.meaning: vertical asymptotes where sine is zero; range (-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)

items.label: Cotangent
items.meaning: vertical asymptotes where tan θ = 0; decreasing between consecutive asymptotes

title: Pythagorean identity
body: \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1
ced_evidence: 3.12.A.1 "Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1"

title: Forms derived from the Pythagorean identity
body: \tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1,\qquad \arcsin x=\arccos\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)
caution: The arcsin–arccos relationship holds only with appropriate domain restrictions.
ced_evidence: 3.12.A.2 "tan²θ = sec²θ − 1 ... arcsin x = arccos(√(1 − x²)), with appropriate domain restrictions"

title: Sum identities for sine and cosine
body: \sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta,\qquad \cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta

title: Difference and double-angle identities come from the sum identities
body: The sine and cosine sum identities can also be used as difference and double-angle identities, and known identities plus algebraic properties can verify additional identities.
ced_evidence: 3.12.B.3 "can also be used as difference and double-angle identities"

title: Polar coordinates (r, θ)
body: Polar coordinates (r, θ) locate a point using the angle θ of a terminal ray in standard position and the signed radial displacement r from the origin.
caution: A negative r means displacement along the line of the terminal ray in the opposite direction. The same point has many polar representations.
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.1 "Polar coordinates of a point are defined as an ordered pair, (r, θ)"

title: Polar to rectangular conversion
body: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.2 "x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ"

title: Rectangular to polar conversion
body: r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad \theta=\begin{cases}\arctan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right), & x>0\\[2mm] \arctan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)+\pi, & x<0\end{cases}
caution: The CED gives no case for x = 0. For x < 0 you must add π to the arctangent.
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.3 "θ = arctan(y/x) for x > 0 or θ = arctan(y/x) + π for x < 0"

title: Complex number in rectangular and polar form
body: a+bi\ \text{for rectangular }(a,b);\qquad (r\cos\theta)+i\,(r\sin\theta)\ \text{for polar }(r,\theta)
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.4 "expressed as (r cos θ) + i(r sin θ)"

title: Meaning of a polar function graph r = f(θ)
body: The graph of r = f(θ) consists of input-output pairs in which the input is an angle measure from the polar axis and the output is a signed radius, and its domain can be restricted by choosing endpoints for the desired angle and radius.
ced_evidence: 3.14.A.1 "input values are angle measures and the output values are radii"; 3.14.A.3

title: Distance from the origin for r = f(θ)
body: How the sign and direction of change of f(θ) determine whether the point's distance from the origin increases or decreases.

items.label: Positive and increasing
items.meaning: distance from the origin is increasing

items.label: Negative and decreasing
items.meaning: distance from the origin is increasing

items.label: Positive and decreasing
items.meaning: distance from the origin is decreasing

items.label: Negative and increasing
items.meaning: distance from the origin is decreasing

caution: Describe the signed radius as increasing or decreasing and the distance as increasing or decreasing. Do not equate the two when r is negative.

title: Relative extrema of a polar function
body: If a polar function changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing on an interval, it has a relative extremum there, corresponding to a point relatively closest to or farthest from the origin.
ced_evidence: 3.15.A.3 "relative extremum ... closest to or farthest from the origin"

title: Average rate of change of a polar function
body: \frac{f(\theta_2)-f(\theta_1)}{\theta_2-\theta_1}
caution: This is the change in signed radius per radian over the interval, and it can be used to estimate function values within the interval.
ced_evidence: 3.15.A.4 "ratio of the change in the signed radius values to the change in θ"; 3.15.A.5
